did.abstract: The Robert Shaw Papers contain annotated musical scores, correspondence, office files pertaining to a variety of topics, photographs, sound recordings, and other materials, by and about the American conductor Robert Shaw (1916-1999).

acqinfo.head: Immediate Source of Acquisition
acqinfo.p: The Robert Shaw Papers were established in the Gilmore Music Library in 2002 by Thomas Shaw and Alex Hitz.

accessrestrict.head: Conditions Governing Access
accessrestrict.p: This collection is open for research. A number of sound recordings from this collection are available to stream online via the Gilmore Music Library's AV access system, Aviary. Links to access these recordings are provided in this finding aid. Yale users can login to Aviary using their Yale University ID, to stream these recordings without restriction. Other users are able to request access to recordings directly through Aviary.

userestrict.head: Conditions Governing Use
userestrict.p: The Robert Shaw Papers are the physical property of the Irving S. Gilmore Music Library of Yale University. Copyrights belong to the composers and authors, or their legal heirs and assigns.

prefercite.head: Preferred Citation
prefercite.p: MSS 86, The Robert Shaw Papers in the Irving S. Gilmore Music Library of Yale University.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: Robert Shaw was born on April 30, 1916 in Red Bluff, California. His father was a clergyman, and he was at first expected to pursue a career in religion rather than music. In his youth he had considerable experience in singing, but he received little formal musical training. At Pomona College, he sang in the Glee Club, and when the conductor had to go on a medical leave of absence, Shaw took over. Fred Waring, a popular band leader, happened to hear the substitute's surprisingly proficient conducting, and he offered Shaw a job. After graduating, Shaw accepted the offer and in 1938 established the Fred Waring Glee Club in New York. Waring's group focused on light music; wanting to take on weightier repertoire, Shaw began conducting the Collegiate Chorale in 1941. He was so successful that within a few years he was teaching choral conducting at Juilliard and at Tanglewood, and preparing choruses for Arturo Toscanini, who called him "The maestro I have been waiting for."

In 1948 Shaw founded the Robert Shaw Chorale, a smaller and more selective group than the Collegiate Chorale. Its many concert tours and best-selling recordings over the next nineteen years made Shaw a household name, and established his reputation around the world as the leading choral conductor of his generation. Meanwhile, despite his rapid success, Shaw was self-conscious about his shortcomings: a limited formal education in music, and a lack of experience as an orchestral conductor. He worked tirelessly to overcome these limitations. In the mid 1940s and early '50s, he took lessons from Julius Herford, Pierre Monteux, and Artur Rodzinski. From 1953 to 1958 he conducted the San Diego Symphony, and from 1956 to 1967, he was the associate conductor of the Cleveland Orchestra, a major job that was also a long apprenticeship under the brilliant but imperious George Szell. Needless to say, Shaw also directed the Cleveland Symphony Chorus.

In 1967, Shaw disbanded the Robert Shaw Chorale and resigned from the Cleveland Orchestra to become the music director of the Atlanta Symphony Orchestra. Atlanta's leaders were determined to show the world that their fast-growing city was no sleepy backwater, and hiring a famous conductor was part of their plan to put Atlanta on the map. (The city acquired its first major league sports teams at about the same time.) The ASO had been a semiprofessional orchestra little known outside the South, but Shaw turned it into a first-rate professional ensemble with a global reputation. The transition was not always smooth, however; Shaw dismissed several veteran musicians, and he nearly resigned in a dispute with the board of directors, some of whom felt that he was performing too much modern music. As one would expect, Shaw also made the ASO Chorus a world leader in its category.

Shaw stepped down from the ASO in 1988, but in retirement he continued to maintain a punishing schedule as a guest conductor, as music director emeritus in Atlanta, and as the leader of several institutes for training choral conductors. He died in New Haven on January 25, 1999; he was in town to see a play directed by his son, Thomas Shaw (Yale Class of 1999).

Shaw married twice. He and his first wife, Maxine Farley, had three children: Johanna, Peter, and Thad. Shaw and his second wife, Caroline Sauls Hitz, had one son, Thomas; Shaw legally adopted Caroline's son by a previous marriage, Alex Hitz.

Shaw released countless recordings, many of which are still available. He received numerous Grammy Awards, honorary degrees, and other distinctions. His life and career are described in Keith Burris's biography, Deep River: The Life and Music of Robert Shaw (Chicago: GIA Publications, 2013), as well as Joseph Musselman's Dear People … Robert Shaw (Bloomington, Indiana University Press, 1979; 2nd edition, Chapel Hill: Hinshaw Music, 1996).

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The largest part of the Robert Shaw Papers consists of Shaw's collection of annotated musical scores. Most works in the standard repertoire are represented by multiple copies, marked up by Shaw at different points in his career. The Papers contain Shaw's extensive office files, which include files on musical topics (including specific composers and compositions); general files (which deal with Shaw's performing career as well as a wide variety of other topics); and general correspondence, including letters from many prominent musicians and other persons of note. The Papers also contain writings (including speeches and Shaw's famous letters to his choruses), photographs, programs, audio and video recordings, and various other materials.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: Organized into 15 series: I. Music II. Books III. General Files IV. Files on Musical Topics V. Correspondence VI. Writings VII. Documents VIII. Photographs and Drawings IX. Clippings X. Scrapbooks XI. Programs XII. Repertoire Indices XIII. Sound Recordings XIV. Audiovisual Material XV. Awards and Miscellaneous Objects

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: More than half of the Robert Shaw Papers consists of annotated musical scores. Most major works appear in multiple versions. When Shaw returned to a piece he had performed earlier in his career, instead of using his old score, he usually obtained a clean score and marked it up from scratch. Shaw annotated his scores in exhaustive detail, using pencils in several colors, and sometimes Post-It notes as well. These scores are a unique window into Shaw's musical thinking, and they also tell us about more practical aspects of his conducting, such as his instrumental cues, and his instructions to the chorus to stand or sit. Certain scores include information about specific performances, such as dates, performers, places, and sometimes even timings.
Shaw usually worked from published editions, but a few manuscripts or manuscript copies also appear. Although this series consists chiefly of scores, it also includes parts for certain works.

Many works for chorus and orchestra are represented by both a full score and a piano-vocal score. When Shaw guest-conducted such works, his assistant often planned for the event by lending an annotated piano-vocal score to the chorus be would be conducting, with the instructions that Shaw's markings should be copied into the singers' own scores.

Shaw was not solely a conductor. He was a prolific choral arranger (usually in collaboration with Alice Parker), and these works also appear in this series, as do the arrangements that Robert Russell Bennett created for the Robert Shaw Chorale.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Titles have been transcribed from the original folders, with some revisions for the sake of clarity and consistency. In a few cases, files include items outside the stated range of dates. (In particular, Sub-series M: 1999-2002 contains many items concerning Shaw's career as a whole.) Many of these files include correspondence relating to the folder's title. Correspondence involving prominent persons has been transferred to Series V, Correspondence, with photocopies retained in the original file. All correspondence that was not filed under a subject has also been transferred to Series V. Photographs have been transferred to Series VIII, Photographs. Appointment books have been transferred to Series VII.F. Files devoted to individual compositions have been transferred to Series IV, Files on Musical Topics.
Certain unfiled materials have been added to the original organization of Shaw's files. These materials are indicated as such.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Includes handwritten notes, photocopies, concert programs, chorus letters, vocal texts and translations, music, and other materials pertaining to specific musical topics. Correspondence involving prominent persons has been transferred to the correspondence series. The folder titles listed here have been transcribed from the original file folders, except in certain cases where they were modified for clarity.
A few boxes (chiefly pertaining to Bach) were processed separately from the others, and thus have box and folder numbers in a separate sequence (Boxes 180-184 and Folders 1-86).

Folders 72-78 and 80 (all in Box 184) contain materials pertaining to works by an alphabetical range of composers, not all of whom are listed in the folder titles. These are entered alphabetically in the following list. Folders 81-86 (also in Box 184) contain materials pertaining to works by a variety of composers, none of them itemized; they appear at the end of the following list, under the title "Music Notes--Miscellaneous."
Certain unfiled materials have been added to the original organization of Shaw's files. These materials are indicated as such.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Robert Shaw's assistants, Edna-Lea ("Eddie") Burruss and Nola Frink, maintained his files. They filed most materials according to event, organization, or subject; these files are kept in Series III. Shaw's files also included large amounts of correspondence that was filed alphabetically by name; they form the core of the present series. In a few cases, institutional correspondence is included here, although most is in the General Files. Letters in the General Files from especially prominent persons have been transferred to this series, with copies retained in the original file. Some names are accompanied by the instruction, "See also Series III, General Files," when other relevant correspondence appears in that series (usually filed under the name of the institution or event with which the person was affiliated). The absence of such a reference after a particular name does not mean that the person does not appear in Series III, however.
Some correspondence appears in Series X, Scrapbooks.

The number of items listed for each correspondent includes letters, cards, and telegrams to or from that person, as well as enclosures (such as clippings, programs, and brochures). In some cases, the enclosures may outnumber the letters.

Incoming and outgoing correspondence is filed together. Many of the outgoing letters were written by Shaw's assistants. Some incoming letters were addressed directly to them, and still others were addressed to Shaw's wife.

Shaw frequently wrote letters of recommendation, as well as letters of tribute (for birthday or retirement celebrations, for example). Such correspondence is usually filed under the name of the person about whom he was writing, rather than the person who solicited the letter.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Shaw's most important writings are his speeches and chorus letters.

This series contain a very large number of speeches, but Shaw was not quite as prolific in this respect as it might seem; he delivered certain speeches (such as "The Conservative Arts") many times, usually with only minor adjustments.

Throughout his career, Shaw customarily wrote a letter each week to the members of his chorus. (His assistants duplicated and mailed them all.) Usually written in the immediate aftermath of a rehearsal, these letters often reflect Shaw's emotions, positive or negative, regarding that rehearsal. They typically contain some combination of praise, criticism, exhortation, musical exercises, historical information, logistical instructions, poems, and jokes.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Most of the photographs are organized into five subseries: VIII.A. Shaw Alone; VIII.B Shaw with One Other Person; VIII.C Shaw with Two Other Persons; VIII.D Shaw with More than Two Other Persons; and VIII.E Photographs without Shaw. Several other subseries are devoted to special events or topics, and to photographic negatives. No attempt has been made to arrange the photographs within each subseries in any particular order. The photographs are numbered, but in certain cases the numbers refer to sets of photographs (usually from the same event), rather than individual photographs. There are some gaps in the numerical sequence. In addition, a few photographs appear out of sequence because they have been transferred from one subseries to another. Oversized photographs are in Box 323. All photographs are black and white except where otherwise noted. This series includes several drawings, which are interfiled with the photographs.
Some photographs may also be found in Series X, Scrapbooks.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: This series is divided into three subseries: A. Cassette Tapes, B. Reel-to-Reel Tapes; and C. Test Pressings.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The Cassette Tapes consist of 326 audio cassettes in 19 tape boxes. The majority of these tapes are recorded from radio broadcasts, including WNYC broadcasts with the Mostly Mozart Festival Orchestra, interviews given to National Public Radio and other stations, rehearsals of works such as the B Minor Mass of Johann Sebastian Bach, live performances, and speeches. The documentation provided with these cassettes is often fragmentary; some are likely to be unlabeled recordings taken from commercially-available LPs.

The tapes focus primarily on recordings made under Shaw's baton, with special emphasis given to Atlanta Symphony Orchestra (ASO), Chorus, and Chamber Chorus performances, as well as to recordings of Shaw guest conducting other orchestras, such as the San Francisco Symphony Orchestra and the Dallas Symphony Orchestra. Notably, the collection includes unreleased concert performances of some of the repertoire that made Shaw's (and the ASO's) fame, including the Requiems by Johannes Brahms and Hector Berlioz.

Many tapes document the performances of prominent instrumentalists from the ASO who worked with Shaw, such as concertmaster William Preucil, and contemporary composers, including ASO composer-in-residence Stephen Paulus. Aside from Shaw performances, the tapes also include some study cassettes assembled by Shaw during concert preparation; these cassettes gather several recordings of particular pieces as conducted by other prominent artists such as George Szell and Simon Rattle.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The Reel-to-Reel Tapes consist of 122 recordings in 5 boxes. The majority of these reels are recorded from live performances and radio broadcasts conducted by Shaw, including many tapes of the Atlanta Symphony Orchestra (ASO), the Cleveland Orchestra, and the Robert Shaw Chorale. Secondarily, the collection includes a limited number of speeches, including a commencement address given by Shaw at the University of Alaska, interviews, including a Russian broadcast from "Voice of America," and festival recordings, with special emphasis on the Casals festivals of 1962 and 1967 and the United Nations Day Concerts of 1963. Much of the information accompanying the reels is fragmentary; accordingly, some commercial dubbings may exist alongside these non-commercial tapes.

The ASO tapes, which constitute the bulk of the collection, document many performances of the orchestra between 1974-1984, including performances of Johann Sebastian Bach's B Minor Mass and the Fifth and Ninth Symphonies of Ludwig van Beethoven. Recordings with other ensembles include tapes made of the memorial concert conducted by Shaw at Kent State University in 1970, where local singers and instrumentalists gathered to perform the Requiem Mass of Luigi Cherubini, in memory of those killed in the Kent State shootings.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The Robert Shaw 78rpm test pressings consist primarily of recordings of the Robert Shaw Chorale, with special emphasis on the ensemble's performances of English and American songs such as "America the Beautiful" and "Oklahoma." The test pressings also document some of Shaw's (primarily classical) work with the Collegiate Chorale and the RCA Victor and NBC Symphony Orchestras, including performances of the B Minor Mass of Johann Sebastian Bach and the Requiems of Luigi Cherubini and Johannes Brahms.

scopecontent.p: Schubert, Mass in G (D. 167). Side 1: Benedictus. Side 2: Agnus Dei (conclusion). Remarks by Ben Hyams: The program is "Invitation to Music" on CBS. The Mass was was performed by the Columbia Chorus and the strings of the CBS Symphony, conducted by Robert Shaw. The soloists were Suzanne Freel, soprano; Ernice Lawrence, tenor; and Paul Ukena, bass. Next week's program will take place at Harvard in conjunction with a symposium on music criticism. Remarks by Sandy Becker: the program was produced under the supervision of James Fassett, directed by Oliver Daniel, with Leo Everett Phillips, technician.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This series includes videos in a variety of formats, arranged chronologically.

did.unittitle: Toscanini and NBC Symphony Orchestra. Beethoven: Symphony No. 9, Part 2

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The NBCTV Broadcast in 1948 of Beethoven's Symphony No. 9, with conductor Arturo Toscanini at Radio City Music Hall featuring the Robert Shaw Collegiate Chorale and soloists Ann McKnight, soprano; Jane Hobson, contralto; Irwin Dillon, tenor; Norman Scott, bass. In the end during the curtain calls, Toscanini brought out the young Robert Shaw along with the soloists.

did.unittitle: Toscanini and NBC Symphony Orchestra. Beethoven: Symphony No. 9, Part 1

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The NBCTV Broadcast in 1948 of Beethoven's Symphony No. 9, with conductor Arturo Toscanini at Radio City Music Hall featuring the Robert Shaw Collegiate Chorale and soloists Ann McKnight, soprano; Jane Hobson, contralto; Irwin Dillon, tenor; Norman Scott, bass. Announcer states that this performance of the Beethoven's Ninth Symphony was Arturo Toscanini's 169th performance as conductor of the NBC Symphony Orchestra and also his 10th full season with the orchestra.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The Art of Robert Shaw is a documentary of his life, work and excerpts showing his style of conducting choruses and coaching singers. It starts with Indiana University where he is a guest lecturer and teacher. The Dean of the Music School, Charles Webb, is interviewed about Shaw. Robert McCoy, teacher at the school states that Shaw could make any ensemble sound like the Robert Shaw chorale. He also goes to Atlanta to rehearse the Atlantic Symphony Orchestra and Chorus. Shaw talks about his personal life. This documentary features excepts of Haydn's Creation.

did.unittitle: Beethoven 9th Symphony. Robert Shaw Conducting the Atlanta Symphony Orchestra & Chorus

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Kaaren Erickson, Soprano; Janice Taylor, Alto; John Garrison, Tenor; John Creek, Bass. After the performance Shaw gives a synopsis of his life and career including studying with Toscanini and the NBC Symphony Orchestra, and George Szell, conductor of the Cleveland Symphony Orchestra, where he was the assistant conductor. Shaw also mentions how Fred Waring brought him to New York with his chorus from Pamona College and eventually he forms the Collegiate Chorale. The video cassette ends with Aaron Copland"s "Fanfare of the Common Man".

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Joyce Kofman, President of the International Choral Festival of Toronto, Canada introduces the head table at a luncheon including Nicholas Goldsmith, Artistic Director of the International Festival who introduces Robert Shaw who then gives a speech.

did.unittitle: 14th Annual Kennedy Center Honors. Honoring Roy Acuff, Betty Comden & Adolf Green, the Nicholas Brothers, Gregory Peck, and Robert Shaw

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The event honors Roy Acuff, Betty Comden and Adolf Green, the Nicholas Brothers, Gregory Peck, and Robert Shaw. The host is Walter Cronkite. CBS broadcast. Before the performance, the honorees are welcomed at the White House by President George Bush and Barbara Bush. The honoreess have famous artists reminisce their relationships. Jean Stapleton who sang in the Robert Shaw Collegiate Chorale expresses a deep gratitude for the opportunity to be chosen to sing with this prestigious ensemble. Robert Shaw's protege, opera singer Sylvia McNair sings "All the Things You Are", the African American Morehouse Chorus from Atlanta peform a Christmas Nigerian song, "Betelehemu" and then finally Handel's "Hallelujah Chorus" is performed by the Atlantic Symphony Orchestra Chorus with Sylvia McNair and William Fred Scott, conductor; Morehouse Chorus, Choral Arts Society of Washington, and the United States Navel Academy Glee Club.

did.unittitle: Martin Luther King Jr. Center. Kingweek, 22nd Annual Ecumenical Service, Ebenezer Baptist Church
Robert Shaw Interviews, conducted by Janet Shapiro & Phillip Byrd
Boston University Baccalaureate Service. Sermon by Robert Shaw

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Robert Shaw, Music Director Emeritus. Shaw conducts the College chorus: Gabriel Faure," Cantique de Jean Racine" followed by his sermon which incorporates theology and the arts.

did.unittitle: Great Performances: Thomas Hampson: I hear America singing

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Hampson, the host, tells the story of the journey of American song starting with Walt Whitman's desire to feature through his poems the history of all parts of America and incorporate poems and song through other poets and composers. Hampson sings Stephen Foster's "Beautiful Dreamer" to open the program. Marilyn Horne sings, "I Dream of Jeanne with the Light Brown Hair" and Joseph Brackett's "Simple Gifts" is sung by Dawn Upshaw, soprano; Jerry Hadley, tenor; and Thomas Hampson, baritone. John Alden Carpenter's, "Ah Love But a Day" is performed by Frederica Von Stade. Some of the other American composers featured are Samuel Barber, Aaron Copland, Charles Ives and Virgil Thomson. PBS Broadcast.
TRT: 86:46. Titled Master. Autographed box with inscription, "For Mr. Shaw with love Thomas Hampson."

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Allison Beth Vulgamore, President of the Atlanta Symphony Orchestra introduces the two choral conductors, Norman Mackenzie and Ann Jones who worked with Shaw. She also introduces William Prescott, a longtime friend of Robert Shaw. Vulgamore acknowledges the Atlanta Orchestra Chorus, Morehouse College Gleeclub, and the Robert Shaw Festival Singers performing in the memorial concert. Sylvia McNair and Marietta Simpson are the soloists. The opening hymn is "O God Our Help in Ages Past". Includes a recording of Shaw reading from an excerpt of Winnie the Pooh in 1948. The highlights of the performance are "As We Gather at the River", Sylvia McNair, soloist; "Sometimes I Feel Like a Motherless Child", Marietta Simpson, soloist; "Trouble of the World", Morehouse College Gleeclub; and the final selection was Handel's "Hallelujah Chorus".

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Tribute prepared for and shown at ACDA Southern Division Convention. It features Shaw himself summarizing his life and career including his relationship with Fred Waring, the formation of the Collegiate Choral, and the inspiration of both Toscanini and Szell. The video features Caroline Shaw whom he married in 1973.
